name: Minoan & Mycenaean Greece
summary: Europe’s first literate civilizations: Minoan Crete built multi-story frescoed palaces at Knossos with indoor plumbing and Linear A, followed by Mycenaean mainland citadel-kings writing early Greek in Linear B and inspiring Homer’s Trojan War epics.
keyFacts: Palace of Knossos frescoes and Thera (Santorini) maritime town
Lion Gate of Mycenae, Treasury of Atreus, and Linear B tablets
evidence: Bibliography pointers only. The cited pages were not opened for this row.

name: Archaic & Classical Greece
summary: Network of over 1,000 Greek poleis across the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Defeated the Achaemenid Persian invasions at Marathon and Salamis, and gave birth to direct democracy, theater, Olympic Games, historiography, and Western philosophy.
keyFacts: Athenian direct democracy (Ecclesia), Parthenon, and Greek Tragedy/Comedy
Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Hippocrates, Herodotus, and Thucydides
evidence: Bibliography pointers only. The cited pages were not opened for this row.

name: Empire of Alexander the Great
summary: In just 13 years, Alexander of Macedon conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire from Greece and Egypt to the Indus River, founding over 20 Alexandrias and inaugurating the three-century Hellenistic synthesis.
keyFacts: Unbeaten campaign from the Hellespont to the Punjab
Foundation of Alexandria in Egypt and spread of Koine Greek across Western Asia
evidence: Bibliography pointers only. The cited pages were not opened for this row.

name: Ptolemaic Egypt & Seleucid Empire
summary: Born from the partition of Alexander’s empire, Ptolemaic Alexandria built the Pharos Lighthouse and the Great Library (where Euclid, Archimedes, and Eratosthenes worked), while the Seleucids ruled from Syria to Persia.
keyFacts: Great Library & Mouseion of Alexandria; Lighthouse (Pharos) of Alexandria
Eratosthenes’ calculation of Earth’s circumference & Rosetta Stone (196 BCE)

name: Byzantine Empire (Eastern Rome)
summary: Direct continuation of the Roman Empire in the Greek-speaking East for more than a thousand years after the fall of Western Rome. Preserved classical Greek literature, codified Roman law, and shielded Europe until 1453.
keyFacts: Corpus Juris Civilis (Code of Justinian) & Hagia Sophia dome
Transmission of Greek manuscripts to Renaissance Italy & Cyrillic heritage to Slavic lands
